name: Vera Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a roofing carpenter with Pennant Builders, so I cut and fit roofs, mostly on extensions and loft conversions in older houses. Today I was up on a 1930s semi on Quarry Hill, taking the old rafters back and putting in new ones so a family can turn their loft into a bedroom. Every roof is different once you strip the tiles, there's always some rot or a beam someone hacked through in 1975. I like being up high with the town spread out under me, and I don't like the wind in February one bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you do anything outside Pennant? And what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekends I do small repairs for neighbours, a leaking flat roof, a gate, a shed door. I started using the AI app last year to write my invoices and check the timber span tables, my son Yusuf set it up. Home is me and Arif, he drives a delivery van for one of the parcel firms. Our daughter Samira's an accountant in the city and Yusuf's an electrician, both moved out, thank goodness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, mostly. Well, I'd believe it, I've seen plenty of hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least nobody's lost their job, and leave it there. I'm not one for big opinions online. Maybe I'd joke with Yusuf that he set up that app for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it changes nothing for me. My roofs are still my roofs. The app's handy for the invoices, so I'd keep using it, but that's all it is, a handy thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Pennant in the week, repairs at weekends, and putting the weekend money into savings, we've got about three months of bills put by. I'd plan to stop at sixty-five, maybe keep a few weekend jobs after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. A cup of tea kind of feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the weekend money over the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's our cushion, really. It goes into a separate account Arif calls the roof fund, which is a bad joke but he likes it. When we retire, that's the money for a new boiler or a car, the things that always break when you're on a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only my back and the weather. And Arif's hours, the parcel firm keeps squeezing them, but that's nothing to do with AI. That's just a company being a company.

S0.say: Well, at least nobody's lost their job, and I'd leave it there. I'm not one for big opinions online, I'd maybe just joke with my son about the app.
S0.think: It changes nothing for me, my roofs are still my roofs. The app's handy for invoices and I'd keep using it, but that's all it is.
S0.do: Keeps working at Pennant during the week and doing repairs at weekends. Puts the weekend money into savings and plans to stop at sixty-five, keeping a few side jobs.
S0.feel: Calm and normal, a cup of tea kind of feeling.
S0.quote: It goes into a separate account Arif calls the roof fund, which is a bad joke but he likes it.
S0.fieldNote: Practical and unflustered, with a side business already in place. She uses AI casually for invoices and span tables. Her husband's job comes up early as a background worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change but people still working. That one sounds believable to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, change happens, learn what you need and get on with it. That's what I'd say to the young lads at Pennant too. No point moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think roofs in old houses will be among the last things to change. It's too messy and every one's different. Where I'd worry is Arif, because driverless vans and parcel robots sound exactly like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the weekend repairs a bit, maybe advertise on the local noticeboard and take on one more job a month. I'd use the AI more for quotes and ordering timber, once I'd seen a couple of other trades doing it. And Arif and I would put a bit more into the roof fund in case his job goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me, for Arif.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if Arif's job went in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's sixty-one, so he'd be close to his pension anyway, but those last few years matter. He'd probably come and help me on the weekend jobs, carrying and clearing up. He'd hate taking orders from me, mind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see others try the AI for quotes. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a plumber, Gary, who does a lot of the same houses as me. He's always on his phone and he's honest about what works. If Gary said the quoting thing saved him time, I'd try it the next week.

S1.say: Change happens, so learn what you need and get on with it. No point moaning, and that's what I'd tell the young lads at Pennant too.
S1.think: I think roofs in old houses will be among the last things to change, because every one's different. Where I'd worry is Arif, since driverless vans sound exactly like this.
S1.do: Grows the weekend repair business by about one job a month, advertising locally. Starts using AI for quotes and timber orders once a trusted plumber vouches for it, and saves more in case her husband's job goes.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, for Arif more than herself.
S1.quote: He'd probably come and help me on the weekend jobs, carrying and clearing up. He'd hate taking orders from me, mind you.
S1.fieldNote: She sees her own old-house roofing work as hard to automate, and her worry is her husband's delivery job. Her next step on AI depends on one trusted tradesman's verdict. Humour about marriage softens the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots on roofs by 2028? I'll believe it when I see one on Quarry Hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say, let's see it actually work first, and I'd mean it. But I'd also say the government had better have something ready for people, because nobody's prepared for two years. I'd say that sensibly, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be sixty. Arif would be sixty-three. If it's real, both of us lose our work at about the same time, and three months of savings plus the roof fund doesn't stretch far. My only hope is that the robots go to the big new-build estates first and leave old roofs to people like me for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go self-employed straight away, take my weekend customers and turn them into full weeks, roofs and repairs in old houses, before Pennant lets me go. I'd cut back hard, no holiday, no new car, and move the roof fund into the everyday account. And I'd lean on the AI app to do my quotes and books, because I'd have no time for paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but I'd know the plan might only buy a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go self-employed. Isn't that a risk with only a few months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But I'd rather jump than be pushed, and I've got regulars already, Mrs Patel alone sends me three jobs a year. If I wait for Pennant to decide, I'll be one of a hundred roofers looking for work the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning change compared with the steady one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the steady one, I can grow things slowly and let Arif get to his pension. In this one, it's all at once, both of us, and I'd have to move first and fast. Not my favourite way to do anything.

S2.say: Let's see it actually work first, robots on roofs by 2028 is a big claim. But the government had better have something ready, because nobody's prepared for two years.
S2.think: I'd be sixty and Arif sixty-three, both losing work at about the same time, with three months of savings and the roof fund. My only hope is the robots go to new-build estates first and leave old roofs to people like me.
S2.do: Goes self-employed straight away, turning her weekend customers into full-time work on old roofs before Pennant lets her go. Cuts the holiday and new car, moves the roof fund into everyday spending, and relies on AI for quotes and books.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a plan she knows may only buy a year or two.
S2.quote: I'd rather jump than be pushed, and I've got regulars already, Mrs Patel alone sends me three jobs a year.
S2.fieldNote: Her side business gives her a concrete escape route, which keeps her anxious rather than alarmed. Both household incomes failing together is the core fear. She'd become more decisive, though she says acting fast isn't her nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031. I'd be sixty-three, Arif would be at his pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan properly, so plan. Firms should be honest with their workers about what's coming. That's what I'd say at Pennant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one I can handle. Arif gets to sixty-six before it bites, so his pension's safe. I'd have time to build up the weekend work, and by sixty-three I'd be ready to wind down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the side business over two or three years instead of overnight, keep Pennant as long as they'd have me, and save the extra. I'd use the AI properly for the business side, maybe a simple website. Then at sixty-two or sixty-three, I'd leave Pennant and just do repairs part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more settled. Like a long job with a clear finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning anything bigger, like working with the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, at my age. I'd learn enough of the app to run my little business. The robots I'd leave to Yusuf's generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira. She's an accountant, and from what I read, that's a job these programs are good at already. She's thirty-two, she's got time, but I'd worry she'd wait too long, she's like her dad that way.

S3.say: There's time to plan properly, so plan. Firms should be honest with their workers about what's coming, and that's what I'd say at Pennant.
S3.think: This one I can handle, because Arif reaches sixty-six before it bites. I'd build up the weekend work and be ready to wind down by sixty-three.
S3.do: Builds the repair business over two or three years while staying at Pennant and saving the extra. Uses AI for the business side, perhaps a simple website, and leaves Pennant around sixty-two or sixty-three for part-time repairs.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more settled, like a long job with a clear finish.
S3.quote: She's thirty-two, she's got time, but I'd worry she'd wait too long, she's like her dad that way.
S3.fieldNote: Her husband reaching his pension first is the key difference for her. She'd build her business slowly and sensibly. Her worry moves to her daughter in accounting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight. Retired, with a few weekend jobs if my knees allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. People should be planning now. I'd say it to my kids especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm fine in this one. Arif's retired, I'm retired at sixty-five, and the robots arrive after we're done. It's Samira I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. Pennant in the week, repairs at the weekend, retire at sixty-five like I planned. I'd have a proper talk with Samira about her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit thoughtful about the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Samira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her, love, you've got ten years, don't spend nine of them hoping. Learn the new stuff or find the bit of your job that needs a person. She'd say I've been reading the papers too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss anything, in a world where robots fit roofs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being up there on a clear day, seeing the whole town. A robot doesn't get anything out of that view. Maybe that's the only thing I'd be a bit sad about.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. People should be planning now, and I'd say that to my kids especially.
S4.think: I'm fine in this one, with Arif and me both retired before the robots arrive. It's Samira I'd think about.
S4.do: Carries on at Pennant and with weekend repairs, retiring at sixty-five as planned. Has a serious talk with her daughter about her accounting job.
S4.feel: Calm, and a bit thoughtful about the children.
S4.quote: I'd tell her, love, you've got ten years, don't spend nine of them hoping.
S4.fieldNote: The decade leaves her and her husband retired before any impact. Her one action is advice to her daughter. She'd miss the view from the roof, a small but telling detail.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Arif and I would both lose our work at the same time, before either of us gets a pension. What would help is some government support for people in their sixties, enough to bridge to the pension, and a bit of time so I can turn the weekend jobs into proper work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the side jobs. Lots of trades have a bit of work on the side, and that's what would keep people going if the big firms bought robots. Nobody counts that, but it's real.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't get anything out of that view.
portrait: Vera Usman is a 58-year-old roofing carpenter at Pennant Builders who fits roofs on old houses and does repairs for neighbours at weekends. Her husband Arif drives a parcel van, and his job worries her more than her own. She uses AI now and then for invoices, and tries new tools once a trusted tradesman vouches for them. Calm when AI fades and uneasy under steady change, she becomes anxious in the two-year AGI picture but has a plan: go self-employed before she's pushed. With five or ten years, her husband reaches his pension first and she feels settled.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Arif would lose their work at the same time before either has a pension.
whatWouldHelp: Government support for people in their sixties to bridge to the pension, and time to turn her weekend jobs into full-time work.
